query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, ALD-deposited alumina coating on refractory high‐entropy alloys will improve high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a continuous, adherent barrier that retards oxygen diffusion, leading to lower oxidation-induced mass gain compared to untreated alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with a multi-principal element composition that, when untreated, forms discontinuous and non-protective mixed oxides during high-temperature exposure in oxygen-rich environments.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin (~50–100 nm) alumina coating using atomic layer deposition (ALD) to pre-form a dense, adherent protective layer on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at approximately 1200°C in an air (oxygen-rich) atmosphere for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, pre-oxidized alumina film on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The ALD alumina layer acts as a diffusion barrier that prevents rapid oxygen ingress, thereby limiting the formation of mixed, non-protective oxide scales and effectively reducing oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ALD-coated alloy will show a significantly reduced mass gain from oxidation (indicative of slower oxidation kinetics) and a more uniform, adherent oxide layer compared to an untreated control under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys typically form uncontrolled, mixed oxides with high mass gain and poor adhesion, resulting in rapid degradation under extreme-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under high-temperature conditions (~1200°C in air for 100 hours); performance may degrade if the coating delaminates due to thermal expansion mismatch or if service conditions exceed the thermal stability of the alumina layer.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness and long-term adhesion at extreme thermal cycling conditions remain to be precisely determined, and there may be variations in performance depending on the specific alloy composition and microstructural features.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the ALD-deposited alumina coating and one set left untreated. Expose both sets to 1200°C in air for 100 hours in a high-temperature oxidation furnace. After exposure, measure the mass gain for each sample and perform cross-sectional microstructural analysis (using SEM/EDS) to assess the continuity and adhesion of the oxide layers.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area to quantify oxidation kinetics.
SEM/EDS imaging of cross-sections to evaluate the continuity and composition of the oxide scales.
Adhesion tests of the oxide layers, e.g., scratch or adhesion tape tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain or do not show a continuous, adherent alumina-based protective layer compared to the untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. frame.system: Refractory high‐entropy alloys used as structural materials at extreme temperatures. Their initial state is that of a multi-principal element alloy that, without specialized modification, suffers from rapid oxidation in high-temperature oxygen‐rich environments.
frame.goal: To improve high-temperature oxygen resistance by ensuring the formation of a continuous and adherent protective oxide layer under extreme service conditions.
frame.limitation: The untreated alloy experiences fast oxygen ingress and uncontrolled oxidation at high temperatures, leading to degradation of mechanical properties.

decision.trend: Early studies largely focused on modifying alloy compositions or processing routes to improve mechanical strength and microstructural stability, but they did not resolve the formation of a continuous, protective oxide scale at high temperatures. The recent work on oxidation mechanisms (e.g., PMC10384371) has shown that in complex high-entropy alloys the oxidation process tends to yield mixed, non-protective scales (such as Mn- or Cr-rich spinels) rather than a uniform barrier. Thus, while compositional modifications without reactive element doping have been attempted, the challenge of spontaneous, self-healing protective oxide formation remains unsolved.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved issue is how to actively induce the formation of a continuous and adherent, thermodynamically stable protective oxide layer that can slow oxygen ingress at extreme conditions (around 1200°C in air for 100 hours) without relying solely on bulk alloy composition changes.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, pre-oxidized alumina-based coating using a technique such as atomic layer deposition (ALD) to create a uniform, adherent protective layer on the alloy surface.
decision.why: Surface treatments can directly engineer the alloy’s interface, bypassing the limitations seen with bulk compositional modifications that failed to produce a stable oxide scale. An ALD-deposited alumina coating has extensive supporting evidence in related high-temperature applications for its ability to act as a diffusion barrier against oxygen. This approach leverages the trend in understanding oxidation pathways in high-entropy alloys and targets the specific need to form a pre-established continuous barrier during extreme service conditions.
